The other day, I found an old shoebox tucked under my bed, its edges frayed with time. Inside were yellowed photos, a half-melted crayon drawing of a stick-figure family, and a single, crumpled note that read: *"Remember the time we built a fort out of couch cushions and pretended it was a spaceship?"* I sat there for a long time, staring at the words, because I couldn’t remember. Not the fort, not the spaceship, not even the exact shade of blue the crayon had been. Just the ghost of a feeling—warmth, maybe, or the quiet thrill of imagination.

It made me think about how memory works like a sieve. Some things slip through, no matter how hard we cling to them. Other things—small, ordinary moments—linger like echoes. Maybe that’s why we hold onto stories, even the ones we can’t quite recall. They’re not just about the past; they’re about the version of ourselves we were, and the version we’re still becoming.

Speaking of becoming, I’ve been trying to learn the piano again. My fingers stumble over the keys like they’ve forgotten their own purpose. But there’s something magical in the struggle—the way a wrong note can still sound like a question, and the right one feels like an answer. It’s humbling, really. To be so bad at something you once loved. But maybe that’s the point. Maybe growth isn’t about getting it right; it’s about showing up, again and again, even when you’re out of tune.

And then there’s the weather. Today, it’s one of those days where the sky is so blue it hurts, and the air smells like cut grass and possibility. I walked to the park and watched a squirrel bury a nut like it was a tiny treasure, like it knew something I’d forgotten: that the world is full of hidden things, waiting to be found. Or maybe it was just being a squirrel. Either way, I envied it a little.

Life is strange like that—full of shoeboxes and squirrels and half-remembered forts. Maybe the goal isn’t to remember everything, but to keep looking, to keep wondering, to keep building, even when the cushions are lumpy and the notes are off-key.
